title: Week 9 · Lesson 26: Pediatric Pathophysiology & Clinical Reasoning — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 9 — Lesson 26: Pediatric Pathophysiology & Clinical Reasoning

FNP-level goal: Recognize how pediatric physiology changes presentation and risk; assess fever, respiratory distress, dehydration, rash, and altered behavior; and identify when outpatient care is unsafe.

Learning Objectives

  • Apply age, weight, development, feeding, urine output, and caregiver observations to pediatric assessment.
  • Recognize respiratory distress, dehydration, sepsis risk, and concerning fever/rash patterns.
  • Distinguish common outpatient syndromes from emergency presentations.

Part 1 — Children Are Not Small Adults

Children have smaller airways, higher metabolic oxygen demand, less physiologic reserve, and age-dependent vital signs. They may compensate with tachycardia and increased work of breathing before hypotension appears. Therefore, normal blood pressure does not guarantee stability.

Appearance, interaction, feeding, urine output, respiratory effort, and trajectory are as important as a single vital sign. Caregiver report that “this is not my child’s normal” is clinically valuable.

Part 2 — Rapid Pediatric Assessment

First assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, and exposure. Observe before touching the child when possible: alertness, consolability, tone, color, work of breathing, and ability to drink/feed. Then obtain age-appropriate vital signs, pulse oximetry when indicated, weight, hydration assessment, and focused source examination.

Emergency findings include apnea, cyanosis, stridor at rest, grunting, marked retractions, inability to feed because of breathing effort, altered responsiveness, seizures, weak pulses, delayed perfusion, hypotension, or rapidly worsening illness.

Part 3 — Respiratory Distress

Small airway narrowing from bronchiolitis, asthma/wheeze, infection, foreign body, or anaphylaxis can produce large increases in resistance. Look for tachypnea, nasal flaring, retractions, head bobbing in young children, grunting, wheeze/stridor, diminished air movement, hypoxemia, fatigue, or inability to speak/feed.

Differentiate upper-airway obstruction (stridor), lower-airway disease (wheeze/prolonged expiration), alveolar disease (crackles/hypoxemia), and nonpulmonary causes such as heart failure, metabolic acidosis, anemia, or sepsis. A quiet chest with exhaustion can be more concerning than loud wheeze.

Part 4 — Fever and Sepsis Reasoning

Fever is a sign, not a diagnosis. Age, immunization status, appearance, source, perfusion, mental status, respiratory effort, rash, urine output, and time course determine risk. Infants and immunocompromised children need lower thresholds for evaluation.

Suspect possible sepsis when infection is accompanied by altered behavior, poor perfusion, mottling, weak pulses, cold extremities, tachycardia out of proportion, abnormal breathing, reduced urine output, or rapid deterioration. Sepsis is an emergency; communicate the suspected source, timeline, vitals, and high-risk features.

Part 5 — Dehydration

Vomiting, diarrhea, fever, poor intake, diabetes, and respiratory distress can rapidly create fluid deficits. Ask about wet diapers/voids, tears, intake, vomiting, stool losses, and activity. Findings can include dry mucosa, sunken eyes, tachycardia, delayed capillary refill, altered skin turgor, lethargy, and abnormal breathing.

Inability to drink, persistent vomiting, lethargy, shock signs, or severe dehydration requires emergency management. The key question is whether circulation and oral hydration can be safely maintained.

Part 6 — Rash and Fever

Rash with fever requires morphology and toxicity assessment. Blanching viral exanthem in a well-appearing child differs from nonblanching petechiae/purpura, mucosal disease, severe skin pain, blistering, hypotension, or altered mental status. The latter patterns require emergency evaluation for invasive infection, hematologic disease, severe drug reaction, or vasculitic processes.

Part 7 — Common FNP Differentials

Cough/wheeze may be viral bronchiolitis, asthma, pneumonia, foreign body, anaphylaxis, or cardiac disease. Abdominal pain can be constipation, gastroenteritis, appendicitis, UTI, intussusception, DKA, or testicular/ovarian pathology. New behavior change can be pain, sleep deprivation, toxin exposure, hypoglycemia, infection, seizure, trauma, or psychosocial stress.

Do not force a child into an adult diagnostic pattern. Growth, development, age, vaccination, medication dosing by weight, and safeguarding context matter.

Part 8 — FNP Clinical Reasoning Case 1

A 10-month-old with cough has nasal flaring, subcostal retractions, grunting, poor feeding, and decreasing wet diapers. Reasoning: respiratory distress plus dehydration risk. Disposition: emergency evaluation; do not manage as a routine URI.

Part 9 — FNP Clinical Reasoning Case 2

A 4-year-old has fever, lethargy, cold mottled extremities, delayed capillary refill, and a rapidly progressive purpuric rash. Disposition: emergency transfer for possible sepsis/serious invasive illness.

FNP High-Yield Framework

Observe first: appearance, breathing, interaction, feeding, and perfusion.
Respiratory red flags: apnea, cyanosis, stridor at rest, grunting, severe retractions, fatigue, poor feeding.
Dehydration red flags: lethargy, poor perfusion, very low urine output, inability to drink, persistent vomiting.
Fever/rash red flags: toxic appearance, nonblanching rash, altered mental status, shock signs, or rapid progression.
